title: The Spies’ Report
lead: Two people of faith can see the future differently than ten voices of fear.
questions: In what area is your “common sense” really fear dressed up as realism?
Which of your convictions, outvoted by others, is waiting for its time, and are you holding on to it like Caleb, without bitterness?
What decision are you making right now, and is there room in your calculations for the one factor the ten left out?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Israel was a few days’ march from its goal. The forty years of wandering didn’t exist yet, and they never had to happen; what decided them was not an army or a famine, but a report. For forty days twelve spies looked over the same land, and they came back with a cluster of grapes so big it took two men to carry it on a pole. One experience, two opposite reports. Facts don’t speak for themselves; the key is the interpretation, written either by faith or by fear.

The majority report started out honestly: the land really was flowing with milk and honey. Then came the “nevertheless”: the people are strong, the cities fortified, giants. None of it was a lie. The ten didn’t lie about the facts; they lied about the proportions. A moment later the same land that was flowing with milk “devours its inhabitants.” And at the end came the key sentence: “we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (KJV). How did they know what the people there thought of them? The text doesn’t say what they based that conclusion on. But they passed off their own picture of themselves as an assessment by the enemy. Years later Rahab of Jericho would show that at least that city was trembling before Israel.

That night the people wept and wanted to go back to Egypt. Two men stood up against everyone, Joshua and Caleb: “If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land… the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them!” They didn’t deny the facts; they had seen the same things. The difference was in who they included in the calculation: the ten counted themselves and the giants; the two also counted God. The crowd wanted to stone them. A majority can be a measure of strength, but never a measure of truth. The generation of fear got what it had shouted for itself, “if only we had died in this wilderness!”, spread out at a year for every day of the spying. But Caleb, a man with “a different spirit,” stayed faithful for forty years to the faith that had been outvoted, and in his old age he picked for himself precisely the hill country with the giants. Fear in a community rarely says, “I’m afraid.” It says, “Let’s be reasonable.” But the minority with God turned out to be the only majority that counted.

Today’s reading opens the section “There Is Hope When Faith Is in the Minority.” The first of these stories took place a few days’ journey from the Promised Land. The Wilderness of Paran, the border of Canaan, not quite two years after leaving Egypt. The entire forty years of wandering that we associate with this book doesn’t exist yet, and it never had to happen. What made it happen was not an army or a famine. The culprit was a report.

sections.heading: Whose Idea Was It?
paragraphs: The book of Numbers begins this story with God’s instruction: “Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan.” But years later, when Moses retells it to the next generation, he adds a detail we don’t see here: “Then all of you approached me and said, ‘Let us send men ahead of us to search out the land.’” Deuteronomy shows that the initiative came from the people. God didn’t need a report on a land He Himself had promised; He agreed to the spying because the people needed it for their own peace of mind. The consequences of that permission would show up forty days later. Anyone who sends out spies to a place where they already have a promise is announcing that they will decide after the report.

sections.heading: Twelve Men, One Land
paragraphs: “Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites.” It’s worth pausing over the grammar of that sentence: the land which I am giving. Not “which I might give you if the reconnaissance goes well.” The spying wasn’t meant to decide whether Israel would go in, only how. Twelve went, all of them leaders, one from each tribe. Before they set out, Moses did one thing that looks like a formality but is really a confession of faith: he changed the name of his trusted aide Hoshea son of Nun to Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.” He sent a man out to spy with the answer written into his name, before anyone had seen the first fortified city. Centuries later, in its Greek form, that same name would belong to the One who would lead His people into a better land. For forty days they went through the country and came back with physical evidence that took two men to carry: a cluster of grapes on a pole from the Valley of Eshcol. They all saw the same things: the same cities, the same people, the same grapes. One experience came back to the camp, and two opposite reports. Facts don’t speak for themselves. They always come carried by someone’s interpretation, written either by faith or by fear.

sections.heading: Nevertheless
paragraphs: The majority report starts out honestly: “indeed, it is flowing with milk and honey. Here is some of its fruit!” And then comes the word that would define the story of that generation: nevertheless. “Nevertheless, the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified.” Everything after “nevertheless” was true. The people really were strong, the cities fortified, the descendants of Anak tall. The ten spies didn’t lie about a single fact. They missed the truth in the proportions. The Hebrew calls their report by a word meaning slander, a bad report. And the text shows how that bad report grows the longer they talk: they started with a land flowing with milk and honey, and a moment later the same land “devours its inhabitants.” A land flowing with milk and a country that eats people are contradictory reports. Fear doesn’t lie outright, but it draws a caricature of reality, and then with every sentence it adds a little more. There’s a reason the old proverb says fear has big eyes.

sections.heading: Like Grasshoppers
paragraphs: At the end of the majority report is a sentence that is the key to this whole story: “we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (KJV). That second half should stop any careful reader. How did they know what the inhabitants of Canaan thought of them? The text doesn’t say what they based that conclusion on. They felt small themselves, attributed that feeling to the enemy’s eyes, and then reported it to the people as intelligence findings. Forty years later, Rahab of Jericho would tell the spies there that “the fear of you has fallen on us.” The Canaanites were trembling before Israel at exactly the time Israel felt like grasshoppers beside them. The ideas we have about ourselves can pass themselves off as facts. What I think others think of me is usually what I think of myself, dressed up as someone else’s voice. Communities can have trouble with their self-image, too: we’re small, there’s only a handful of us, who would ever listen to us? And just like that report, they present it as objective data about the world, even though no one outside ever said it. Meanwhile, on the other side of the wall, things may be just as they were in Jericho: people waiting for someone to come with real hope, and not seeing grasshoppers at all.

sections.heading: Two Against Everyone
paragraphs: That night “the whole congregation lifted up their voices and cried out, and that night the people wept.” Out of the weeping a political program was born: “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt.” Then two of the twelve, Joshua and Caleb, stood before the crowd with their clothes torn: “The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land… Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not be afraid of the people of the land.” Notice what isn’t in that speech: there is no denial of the facts. Joshua and Caleb don’t say the cities are small and the descendants of Anak are short. They saw the same things the others did. The difference isn’t in the data but in who else they included in the calculation: “the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them!” The ten counted themselves and the giants. The two counted themselves, the giants, and God. The community’s response was immediate: “the whole congregation threatened to stone Joshua and Caleb.” And at exactly that moment, as the crowd reached for stones, “the glory of the LORD appeared to all the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting.” God steps in when He judges it right: not when His people lose a vote, but when a mob starts to threaten them. That is the arithmetic of this scene: two against ten on the committee, two against six hundred thousand in the square. A majority can be a measure of strength, but never a measure of truth.

sections.heading: A Different Spirit
paragraphs: About Caleb, God gives one of the most beautiful testimonies ever given about a person in Scripture: “My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly, I will bring him into the land he has entered.” But before that word about Caleb was spoken, something happened without which this book would have had no sequel. The Lord told Moses He would destroy this people and make a greater nation out of Moses himself. But Moses reminded God of His own words, “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion,” and prayed, “Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion.” The answer came at once: “I have pardoned them as you requested.” Forgiveness is free and complete, but it doesn’t undo every consequence: the generation of the spies wasn’t wiped out on the spot, as God’s anger had warned, but it didn’t enter the land either; it lived on and ate manna to the end of its days. There are sins God forgives whose consequences still have to be walked through on foot, year after year. In that case forgiveness changes not the route but the company: you cross the same desert, but with God, not against Him.

God said Caleb had a different spirit. Not a different temperament, not steadier nerves, not more optimism. The text doesn’t say whether Caleb felt no fear or bitterness. What it does show is that he made a different decision about whom to believe, and stayed faithful to it for decades, including all the years of wandering with the generation that had rejected his report. When he finally entered the land as an eighty-five-year-old man, he asked Joshua for his share and chose the hill country of Hebron, the one with the descendants of Anak, the very place that old report had been loudest about. Faith in the minority has to be able to wait for decades without bitterness. Caleb could.

sections.heading: A Year for Each Day
paragraphs: The sentence on that generation has a bitter symmetry: “In keeping with the forty days you spied out the land, you shall bear your guilt forty years, a year for each day.” Forty days of spying, forty years of desert. And God prefaces the sentence with words that send a shiver down your spine: “I will do to you exactly as I heard you say.” They had cried out: if only we had died in this wilderness. They were taken at their word. Their children, who they said would become plunder, entered the land; they themselves got exactly what they had shouted in their night of panic. The next morning they still tried to reverse it all: they got up early, admitted their sin, and set off for the hill country to take the land on their own, against the word they had just heard. They came back beaten. The courage that yesterday would have been obedience was, today, only stubbornness. Faith can’t be made up for with a burst of effort at the wrong moment; faith is obedience at the right one.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story is in the Bible so that we would know that a community’s future doesn’t depend on the vote count, but on who is right before God. Two people saw clearly, ten were blinded by fear, and the truth that was outvoted didn’t stop being true; it waited forty years and entered the land with the children of those who had wept. It’s also worth remembering what the voice of fear sounded like: it didn’t sound like cowardice. It sounded like realism, like concern for families, like a sober assessment of the situation. Fear in a community of believers almost never says, “I’m afraid.” It says, “Let’s be reasonable.” And one more thing: if today you are standing in faith as part of a minority, in your family, at work, in your own church, remember that in this story the minority with God turned out to be the only majority that counted. The point isn’t to distrust the majority on principle, or to call every bit of stubbornness faith; the next morning we saw that stubbornness without the Almighty loses just as surely as fear without Him. The point is that in every calculation we make before a decision, there should be room for that one factor the ten spies left out.
